name: Madhu and Kaitabha
role: Asura pair in the Devi Mahatmya and the Mahabharata
summary: Madhu and Kaitabha are two asuras said to arise as Vishnu rests on the cosmic waters. They trouble Brahma and are ended by Vishnu, so he is called Madhusudana.
about: Many Puranas say that Madhu and Kaitabha formed from the earwax of Vishnu as he slept in yoganidra, and the Devi Mahatmya places them in its very first episode. A lotus grows from Vishnu's navel and Brahma sits on it. The pair become fearsome and threaten Brahma. In the Devi Bhagavata Purana they earn a boon that they may die only by their own consent, and they steal the Vedas. Brahma praises the Goddess, who stirs Vishnu awake in the Devi Mahatmya. In the best known telling Vishnu invites them to ask for a boon, they offer one in pride, and he asks for their deaths. They ask to be killed where there is no water, so he places them on his thighs and ends them with his discus. In the Bhagavata Purana he takes the form Hayagriva to recover the Vedas.
kidSummary: Madhu and Kaitabha were two strong asuras born from Vishnu while he slept on the ocean. They tried to cause trouble for Brahma and even took the Vedas. In the end Vishnu stopped them with a clever idea, and he got the names Madhusudana and Kaitabhajit.

story.title: Born while Vishnu slept
story.text: While Vishnu rested on the waters, two asuras, Madhu and Kaitabha, were born from his earwax.

story.title: Brahma on the lotus
story.text: A lotus grew from Vishnu's navel. Brahma sat on it to plan the world, and the two asuras came to him.

story.title: A boon and a theft
story.text: They did tapas to the goddess and earned a boon, and then they took the Vedas to the underworld.

story.title: Vishnu wakes
story.text: In the Devi Mahatmya, Brahma praised the goddess Yoganidra, who let Vishnu wake (in the Devi Bhagavata, Brahma praises Vishnu). Then the two fought for a very long time without either winning.

story.title: A clever request
story.text: When the asuras boasted and offered him a boon, Vishnu asked for their lives.

story.title: The dry place
story.text: They asked to be ended where there was no water. Vishnu raised his thighs above the sea as dry land and won, and so he is called Madhusudana.

teaches: Cleverness can be stronger than strength
Knowledge, like the Vedas, is worth guarding

facts.text: Many Puranas say that Madhu and Kaitabha were born from the earwax of Vishnu while he slept in yoganidra.
In one account Vishnu made two dewdrops on the lotus. The drop sweet as honey became Madhu, with the quality of tamas (darkness), and the hard drop became Kaitabha, with rajas (activity).
In the Bhagavad Gita, Arjuna addresses Krishna by the name Madhusudana, an old epithet of Vishnu that recalls this very story.
In the Devi Bhagavata Purana, the goddess gave them a boon that death could come to them only with their own consent.
In the Devi Bhagavata Purana, the earth is called Medini because the marrow of the slain pair mixed with it, and the text itself adds that the earth was already there before them.
In the Devi Bhagavata telling, the boon meant the pair could die only if they wished it, so Vishnu meditated on the Goddess, who told him only trickery could work.
In the Devi Bhagavata Purana, they asked to be killed anywhere except in water. Vishnu raised his thighs above the sea as dry land, and ended them there with his discus.
In the Padma Purana, Madhu hid in darkness and used illusion to drop a hundred mountains on Vishnu, who cut off his head with the Sudarshana; Brahma and Shiva then gave Vishnu the name Madhusudana.
When the pair swelled to a thousand yojanas in the Devi Bhagavata telling, Vishnu made his thighs larger still, laid them across his lap and ended them there.
In a telling linked to the Bhagavata Purana, the slain pair's bodies split into twelve pieces: two heads, two torsos, four arms and four legs.
The Mahabharata says the pair had a son named Dhundhu, who sought revenge on Vishnu and was killed by King Kuvalashva and his sons.
In the Devi Mahatmya, Brahma asks the goddess Yoganidra, the divine sleep itself, to release Vishnu so he can wake and face Madhu and Kaitabha; it is among the earliest texts to name her.
In the Mahabharata, the pair's son Dhundhu lay hidden in a cave under a sea of sand called Ujjalaka, and Kuvalashva's sons dug for seven days to reach him before his fire killed them.
In the Devi Bhagavata telling the brothers took turns: while Madhu fought Vishnu, Kaitabha rested, then they swapped, until Vishnu himself was worn out.

Born in water, the pair grew up and walked on its surface, proud and wondering how the great flood began. The Goddess appeared, taught them the Vagbija mantra, and they worshipped her for a thousand years.
Terrified when the asuras stole the Vedas and attacked him, Brahma ran to Vishnu, who lay in deep contemplative sleep, and praised him until he woke, says the Devi Bhagavata.
Devotees ask Hayagriva's blessing when they begin studying any subject, sacred or secular, and special worship is held on the August full moon and on Mahanavami.
In the Mahabharata passage on Hayagriva, after the two danavas are slain and the Vedas returned, Narayana gives Brahma the highest understanding of creation, and Brahma then makes the worlds.
Early evidence of Hayagriva worship goes back to about 100 BCE, when people honoured the horse for its speed, strength and intelligence.
The Puranic Encyclopaedia notes two birth stories: earwax in the Devi Bhagavata, and two water drops in Mahabharata Shanti Parva chapter 348.
